title: How the US can achieve nuclear energy dominance at home and abroad
gist: A policy blueprint for US civil nuclear expansion arguing that hourly electricity pricing over-rewards intermittent wind and solar at baseload's expense, that redirecting 10 percent of the $1.4 trillion ESG allocation to financial institutions into nuclear project finance could unlock ~$400 billion, and that EXIM reauthorization, a $1bn/year US equity revolving fund, spent-fuel take-back, and exported operational expertise are needed to beat Russian and China's all-in-one nuclear export model.

insights.claim: Hourly and daily electricity pricing systems create perverse incentives leading to over-investment in fluctuating wind and solar supply, redirecting investment away from reliable baseload generators and creating grid stress.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Any reform of hourly market clearing toward firm-capacity payments would materially re-rate nuclear and other baseload asset economics.
insights.locator: Update market mechanisms to incentivize the firm, baseload power

insights.claim: California's solar-driven 'duck curve' and Europe's price swings from negative to exorbitant depending on solar and wind fluctuations are cited as evidence that current market incentives harm consumers and industrial users alike.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Negative-to-spike power price volatility is the stated symptom to watch; it strengthens the case for firm capacity and storage revenue streams.
insights.locator: California’s solar-driven “duck curve”

themes.theme: Unlocking capital: ESG rebalancing and Wall Street's absence

insights.claim: While some nuclear energy start-ups have attracted single-digit billions of dollars, Wall Street has yet to step into nuclear project development finance in a serious way.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The venture-funded nuclear story has outrun the project-finance story; the bottleneck is construction capital, not startup equity.
insights.locator: Involve Wall Street

insights.claim: Of the global $3.9 trillion in ESG-focused investment funds, nearly $1.4 trillion (35 percent) is invested in financial institutions and instruments, and rebalancing 10 percent of that into nuclear project finance could raise nuclear investments by nearly $400 billion.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Quantifies a ~$400bn potential capital pool for nuclear if ESG mandates reallocate — a size that would transform the sector's supply chain.
insights.locator: One good use of the global $3.9 trillion

insights.claim: Key institutions including the European Union and the World Bank now group nuclear into the 'green' or 'carbon-free' investment category, removing a formal barrier to ESG capital flowing into nuclear.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Taxonomy reclassification is the precondition for the capital rotation; the mandate constraint has already been lifted, so flows can follow.
insights.locator: Key institutions like the European Union and the World Bank

themes.theme: Export finance is the competitive chokepoint

insights.claim: Reauthorizing the US Export Import Bank must be a top congressional priority because without EXIM, US nuclear exports simply will not be able to compete with other exporters such as Russia and China.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: EXIM reauthorization is a discrete legislative catalyst for US reactor vendors' international order books.
insights.locator: Reauthorize the US Export Import Bank (EXIM)

insights.claim: Congress is already reviewing draft legislation that separates high-dollar nuclear loans from EXIM's general default cap, an important step to let the EXIM team move more aggressively on nuclear loans.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A specific bill provision to track: carving nuclear out of the default cap directly expands financeable deal size.
insights.locator: Congress is already reviewing draft legislation

insights.claim: A US government revolving fund of one billion dollars a year for five years would be enough to leverage local capital and take at least twenty-five individual reactor projects — five per year — through feasibility and front-end engineering to final investment decision, with the equity stake later sold to private investors likely at a profit.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Puts a price on unlocking 25 international reactor FIDs — $5bn of catalytic public equity — a cheap policy lever with recycled capital.
insights.locator: Establish a US government revolving fund

insights.claim: The State Department's FIRST program for small modular reactor infrastructure has a fifty-country wait list for bilateral programs even with cash and in-kind contributions from partners including Argentina, Canada, Finland, Japan, Korea, and the UK.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A fifty-country queue is a concrete measure of latent global SMR demand that currently has no US delivery channel.
insights.locator: Increase funding for capacity development activities

insights.claim: Pooling several projects in adjacent markets using the same technology vendor mitigates first-of-a-kind risk and lets participants share lessons learned, as modeled by the State Department's SMR Pan-Regional Interest Nuclear Group (SPRING) program for prospective US SMR customers in Central Europe.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Fleet-scale multi-country ordering is the mechanism that converts SMR cost curves from first-of-a-kind to nth-of-a-kind — watch for regional order clusters.
insights.locator: Protect international projects from cost overrun and technology risk

insights.claim: The United States should abandon the once-through nuclear fuel model and update regulations to allow the return of spent fuel from outside the country, since some US competitors already offer spent fuel take-back programs that make them more appealing partners.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Take-back and recycling is a differentiator in export bids; regulatory change here would open a new US fuel-services revenue line.
insights.locator: Abandon the “once-through” nuclear fuel model

insights.claim: New US business models are emerging that could make spent-fuel recycling profitable, so enabling domestic recycling and take-back programs could give the United States a competitive edge.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Reprocessing economics turning positive would create an investable segment that has historically been uneconomic in the US.
insights.locator: New US business models, however, are emerging

insights.claim: Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz has made clear that energy security requires diversity of supply across every energy supply chain including nuclear, justifying a larger domestic nuclear fuel bank plus secure 'branch office' depots with trusted allies.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A live Hormuz closure is being used to justify strategic stockpiling beyond oil and gas — expect enrichment and conversion capacity to be treated as strategic assets.
insights.locator: Build a larger nuclear fuel bank at home

themes.theme: Operations, licensing, and standards as US advantage

insights.claim: The US reactor fleet operates at the highest capacity factor of any in the world, over 92 percent, making US operational expertise key to compelling financial results for partner countries.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A hard, quantified US advantage that is currently unmonetized in exports; operations-and-maintenance services are the underexploited margin pool.
insights.locator: Incentivize US reactor operators to share their expertise globally

insights.claim: US technology vendors often lack operational counterparts to support partner countries even when they have a construction partner, putting US projects at a competitive disadvantage against Russia and China which offer all-in-one exports bundling construction, financing, and operational services.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Bundled build-finance-operate is the winning export product; US vendors need consortium partners to compete for sovereign reactor tenders.
insights.locator: This puts US projects at a competitive disadvantage

insights.claim: Industry is ahead of government in developing micro-reactors for remote communities and industrial operations and small modular reactors to power global shipping, so the US government must lead in establishing global safety and nonproliferation standards for transportable and civil maritime reactors to secure commercial and security advantage.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Nuclear-powered commercial shipping is an emerging segment gated by absent standards — standard-setting timing is the gating item for that market.
insights.locator: Accelerate work on setting safety and nonproliferation standards

insights.claim: Nuclear diplomacy instruments already exist and should be leveraged — 123 Agreements required under US law to permit nuclear technology and material exports, intergovernmental agreements to help US firms secure projects, and memoranda of understanding to regularize government-to-government engagement.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: New 123 Agreements are the observable precondition for any US reactor export deal — track signings as the leading indicator.
insights.locator: Strengthen nuclear diplomacy

insights.claim: Supporting the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's work to rationalize and speed licensing is key to promoting US technology exports, because the NRC sets the world's standard for safe, secure, responsible licensing and reforms must both respond to technological developments and strengthen global trust in the NRC.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: NRC licensing throughput is the domestic build-rate constraint and a soft-power export asset; reform pace is the key schedule variable for US SMR developers.
insights.locator: Support the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s (NRC) work

insights.claim: President Trump at the beginning of his second term set an expansive agenda for accelerating deployment of new nuclear energy at home and advancing US industry leadership abroad, doubling down on the previous administration's goal to increase nuclear capacity.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Bipartisan continuity on nuclear capacity targets reduces policy-reversal risk for long-duration nuclear investments.
insights.locator: At the beginning of his second term

insights.claim: The proposed nuclear measures are mutually reinforcing, and instituting all simultaneously is unnecessary — starting with three or four would position US industry to deliver on restoring nuclear leadership.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Signals partial-implementation is sufficient, so incremental policy wins (EXIM, NRC reform) still move the sector thesis.
insights.locator: Delivering on US nuclear leadership
